ABSTRACT

METEOROLOGICAL DRIVERS OF PM10 VARIABILITY IN CHATTOGRAM CITY: A SEASONAL ANALYSIS OF PRECIPITATION, RELATIVE HUMIDITY, TEMPERATURE, AND WIND SPEED (2022–2025)

Journal: Journal CleanWAS (JCleanWAS)
Author: Justine Bundi, Joan Nyika, Ednah Onyari
This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

Doi: 10.26480/jcleanwas.02.26.68.74

IThe study focuses on the impact of important meteorological parameters (precipitation, wind speed, relative humidity, and temperature) on PM10 levels in the second-largest city in Bangladesh, namely Chattogram, as well as being a major port and industrial city. The monthly PM10 data available from the Department of Environment, Bangladesh and NASA POWER meteorological data were analyzed during 48 months (2022-2025). PM10 concentrations were significantly higher during winter (mean 123.58 µg/m³, SD 57.66) and premonsoon (mean 102.40 µg/m³, SD 67.57) than during the monsoon season (mean 39.56 µg/m³, SD 28.01), reaching a maximum of 238.70 µg/m³ in January 2024. The one-way ANOVA showed that there is a statistically significant seasonal effect (F(2,37) = 10.22; p < 0.001; η² = 0.356). Pearson correlation analysis showed that PM10 was significantly and negatively associated with precipitation (r = −0.412, p = 0.004), wind speed (r = −0.407, p = 0.004), relative humidity (r = −0.392, p = 0.006), and temperature (r = −0.365, p = 0.011). A combination of precipitation, wind speed and relative humidity as a combined multiple linear regression was significant (F(3,44) = 3.55, p = 0.022, R² = 0.195), but none of the three meteorological variables was individually significant (all p > 0.05); a pattern consistent with strong intercorrelation between the meteorological variables (VIF 2.96–4.27). The results show that the seasonal timing, rather than individual meteorological factors, is the major and most consistent factor explaining PM10 variability in Chattogram, and that individual meteorological factors work synergistically. The findings are supportive of seasonally adaptive AQM, focusing on emission control in winter and pre-monsoon dry season.
